author: Marissa Kraus
title: Denver Summit FC celebrates Santa Fe Yards stadium groundbreaking - NewsBreak
text:
By Marissa Kraus ,
3 hours ago Janine Sonis remembers driving by the Santa Fe Yards at South Broadway and I-25 countless times, wondering what it would become.
Her question has been answered.
The Highlands Ranch native and Denver Summit FC defender on Thursday sat at the empty lot to witness the groundbreaking of the Summit’s future permanent stadium. Sonis joined her team, civic leaders, community partners and club supporters in a ceremony to commemorate the event.
“There are not enough words to express what today means as a Colorado native and person involved in the club,” Sonis said. “The level of investment is something I’ve never seen, and to be a part of it is incredibly special.”
People write messages on a sheet of paper that will be placed in a time capsule during a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Santa Fe Yards stadium on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (Stephen Swofford, The Denver Gazette) Thursday’s ceremony included a land blessing and remarks from Summit FC President Jen Millet, club owner Rob Cohen and Mayor Mike Johnston , along with a fireside chat with Sonis and defender Eva Gaetino. Music performances by Las Dahlias Mariachi and the 14ers supporter group added to the festivities.
“Surreal” was the word of the day.
An excavator raising a Summit flag behind the ceremony stage symbolized what will be center field. A theme throughout the ceremony was building something of their own.
“As women and girls, we are taught implicitly, and sometimes explicitly, not to take up too much space,” Millet said. “What women lacked was investment, not talent. For decades, the energy, passion and economic power of this game have been bursting at the seams of borrowed venues, borrowed dates, borrowed locker rooms under somebody else’s lights.
“So, today, we aren’t asking for a room of our own inside someone else’s venue. We’re standing in the heart of downtown Denver, surrounded by the skyline and the mountains and the pulse of the city, to break ground on a stadium built by us, for us.”
Much of the funding will come from taxpayers.
The groundbreaking came after Denver City Council approved final funding for the stadium in December. The city council pledged $70 million as a ceiling for the Summit stadium project, but that bill could cost nearly $20 million more, The Denver Gazette previously reported . Early estimates put the stadium price tag between $150 million and $200 million, but it could reach more than $300 million.
Mortenson will begin construction for the 14-acre sports and entertainment district in the coming weeks, with a targeted completion set for the end of 2028. With this timeline, the Summit anticipates playing most of its 2028 regular-season home matches at its current temporary 12,000-seat Centennial Stadium.
A row of player photos hangs from the “bridge to nowhere” that will become a thoroughfare from the light rail into the stadium during a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Santa Fe Yards stadium on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (Stephen Swofford, The Denver Gazette) The future stadium’s updated design by Populous features a fixed seating capacity of 12,500 with expanded standing-room-only safe-standing areas bringing the total venue capacity to 13,000, according to a news release. The updated design “prioritizes fan experience, atmosphere and accessibility,” with social spaces for fans and expanded terraces.
“It’s a goosebump day,” said Elizabeth Erfling, Mortenson project executive. “It’s exciting for our team, our city and for my daughter who plays soccer. It’s a momentous investment in women. Being in construction, people have invested in me that way, so there are a lot of parallels.”
Upon completion, it will be the second stadium built exclusively for an NWSL team after the Kansas City Current’s 11,500-seat CPKC Stadium opened in 2024. Kansas City recently announced its approval for a $185 million expansion that will raise the stadium’s capacity to 18,000.
“It’s a bit surreal for me,” Denver captain Lindsey Heaps said. “Growing up, I didn’t believe this would happen. It brought tears to my eyes. I feel so lucky and grateful they brought me back here, and I’m proud and happy to have a women’s-specific stadium.”
Heaps was recently named to the 26-player USWNT training camp roster for two October matches, one of six Summit players to earn call-ups for the upcoming international window.
Summit FC Players throw shovels of dirt for a photo op during a groundbreaking ceremony for the new Santa Fe Yards stadium on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. (Stephen Swofford, The Denver Gazette) Heaps and Sonis are two of the five Colorado natives on the Summit roster, along with Jordan Nytes, Ally Brazier and Meg Boade. At the groundbreaking, both Heaps and Sonis talked about not having a women’s team to look up to growing up and how they hope to inspire young boys and girls.
Having a stadium of their own was an unlikely dream — Thursday marked the beginning of it becoming reality.
“Colorado has an incredible track record of producing not just soccer players, but great athletes in general,” Sonis said. “To have the ability for young girls and boys to have both the Rapids and us to look up to, they are spoiled for choice. It creates a whole new level of dream and ability for a young girl to see a hometown pathway for them.”
